## Abstract
A vast body of empirical literature documents the existence of short-term momentum and medium-term mean reversion in various financial markets. However, few theoretical models explain these two common phenomena. A Markov model, wherein the return process randomly switches between bull and bear states, can reproduce many stylized facts of financial asset returns, excluding the mean reversion. An important limitation of the Markov model is that the state termination probability does not depend on age.
We develop a semi-Markov model wherein, following the empirical evidence, the state termination probability increases with age. We demonstrate that this model induces short-term return momentum and subsequent reversal. We calibrate our model to real-world data and show that the empirical results agree with our theoretical model.

# Inside System One AI: Building Decision-Native Models with Calibrated Confidence
### The fundamental problem: prediction is not the same as knowing how reliable the prediction is
That assumption is called **calibration**.

*Calibration is therefore* ***not primarily about whether a model is correct on one particular example**.

### RLCD and the concept of epistemic uncertainty
A model can be perfectly calibrated on one distribution and badly calibrated after distribution shift.

Therefore a serious RLCD system needs evaluation across:

```
in-distribution data
out-of-distribution data
temporal drift
rare cases
adversarial cases
subgroups
new domains
```

### Calibration does not mean the model cannot be wrong
If the model produces 10,000 predictions around 0.70 and approximately 7,000 are correct, then the model can be well calibrated even though 3,000 individual predictions are wrong.

Therefore:

```
calibrated
```

does not mean:

```
always correct
```

It means:

```
confidence is statistically meaningful
```

This distinction is fundamental when designing automated systems.

**Calibration also does not mean the model is unbiased**

A model could be well calibrated globally while having very different error rates across groups or domains.

The RLCR work provides a **concrete and theoretically motivated method for adding calibration rewards to reasoning-model RL**.

# A tractable framework for analyzing a class of nonstationary Markov models

Lilia Maliar, Serguei Maliar, John B. Taylor, Inna Tsener

We consider a class of infinite‐horizon dynamic Markov economic models in which the parameters of utility function, production function, and transition equations change over time. In such models, the optimal value and decision functions are time‐inhomogeneous: they depend not only on state but also on time. We propose a quantitative framework, called extended function path (EFP), for calibrating, solving, simulating, and estimating such nonstationary Markov models. The EFP framework relies on the turnpike theorem which implies that the finite‐horizon solutions asymptotically converge to the infinite‐horizon solutions if the time horizon is sufficiently large. The EFP applications include unbalanced stochastic growth models, the entry into and exit from a monetary union, information news, anticipated policy regime switches, deterministic seasonals, among others. Examples of MATLAB code are provided.

deepseek.snippet: Every information ecosystem produces beliefs that shape strategic decisions. Both human analysts and AI systems inherit the blind spots of their information sources. We show that LLMs, combined with prediction markets, function as a calibrated instrument for measuring how far ecosystem-induced beliefs deviate from an external reference: LLMs extract the beliefs a text corpus implies, and prediction market price trajectories, anchored at resolution by realised outcomes, provide the calibration reference against which to quantify the deviation. We isolate the bias contribution of specific text through ablation: varying information context while holding the model fixed, with a contaminated model that knows actual outcomes as control. Applied to 111 Ukraine-related prediction markets, comprising approximately 93,000 predictions across four models, we find that English news context systematically biases territorial predictions, wrong 64 to 72 percent of the time when it pushes predictions toward territorial capture. A contaminated model that knows actual outcomes shows the same error rate, indicating that the bias originates primarily in the text. Supplementing with Ukrainian military-analytical sources reduces the bias for all clean models, while absolute-error gains are partial and model-dependent. We show that the distortion originates primarily in the sources, not the models. Consistent across four architectures, it will persist in any system that processes them and propagate into downstream decisions.

Before our search pipeline retrieves anything, it decides how wide to search. “NVDA margins last two quarters” is about one company, so a narrow search over NVIDIA’s documents is enough. “Which companies are decreasing payroll?” names no company, so it needs broad market research: a slower sweep across every company we cover. We used to make this call with a prompted LLM.

Decision models answer a yes/no question like this one with a probability, in a few hundred milliseconds. A decision model can replace the prompted LLM entirely, or it can sit in front of the LLM in a model cascade. In a cascade, the decision model handles most requests itself and escalates to the LLM only when it is uncertain. Either way, the developer has to pick one or more thresholds, and picking them usually means tuning on annotated data.

Calibration can remove that step. A decision model is calibrated when its probabilities mean what they say: of the queries it scores 0.7, about 70% really are yes ([Guo et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599)). A calibrated model’s default threshold of 0.5 is a sensible starting point, and the scores near 0.5 are where it is most likely to be wrong, which is exactly what a cascade should escalate.

Luna needs no tuning but tops out about 5 points lower.

keenable.title: Are Calibrated Decision Models Calibrated on Markets? Geolocated News, Markov Switching and a System One Model for Nasdaq-100 Allocation
keenable.snippet: Portfolio allocation is driven by probabilities of losses, not only by forecasts of the direction (up/down) of the market. A decision model such as Jev returns a probability for a yes/no question and has been reported to be well calibrated on a set of benchmarks. However, the model's calibration against realised market outcomes has not been tested. In this study, every Friday we ask whether the Nasdaq-100 will close lower four weeks later and compare a two-regime Markov-switching model estimated on data from 1990 to 2026, Jev reading weekly headlines and geolocated news features computed with spatial queries in PostGIS, and their combination. A knowledge probe shows that Jev knows events up to late 2024, so we evaluate it on 88 weeks from January 2025 onwards. None of the models predicts the direction better than the historical base rate. A key finding is that raw Jev overestimates the probability of a decline: its mean forecast is 0.48 against an observed frequency of 0.38, and its ECE is 0.10. A prior shift to the historical base rate, which uses no outcomes from the test period, lowers the ECE to 0.015. In contrast, Platt scaling, isotonic regression and the combination with the Markov model all make the forecasts worse. In a half-Kelly allocation, the raw Jev strategy returns 3.1% per year, whereas after the prior shift it returns 14.5%; a simple buy-and-hold strategy in QQQ returns 15.3% per year. The Markov model forecasts large declines (more than 10%) well, with an AUC of 0.81, and its strategy has the highest Sharpe ratio over 1999-2026. Asked about such a large decline (base rate 4%), raw Jev forecasts 16-24% on average, and the same prior shift removes this offset. The practical lesson is that decision-model probabilities must be anchored to the base rate of the market event before they are used to size positions.

keenable.title: Abstract
keenable.snippet:
### Decision model (Jev)
Jev is a “System One” decision model: instead of generating text, it returns a probability for a yes/no question (TypeSafe,, 2026; Deußer et al.,, 2026). We query version typesafe/jev-1.14-20261014 through the OpenRouter Decisions API with one fixed question for all weeks and inputs: *“Given the information available on [date] (a Friday), will the Nasdaq-100 index close lower 4 weeks later than it closed on [date]?”*, with the criteria “closes lower” (true) and “closes at the same level or higher” (false). The output p_t^(Jev) is the probability of “true”. We query Jev with four alternative inputs: (i) the 50 most widely published English-language headlines of the week (25 on economy and markets, 25 on conflict and geopolitics; see Data); (ii) the same headlines plus a JSON object with the GDELT features of the seven regions and their percentiles relative to past weeks; (iii) this JSON object alone; and (iv) a JSON object with Nasdaq-100 returns over 1, 4, 13 and 52 weeks, the 13-week volatility and the drawdown from the 52-week high (no index level, so that the input does not reveal the date). All 373 queries were made on 27 October 2026 and cost USD 0.017 in total (about USD 0.00005 per query).

We tested whether Jev, a decision model advertised as calibrated, gives calibrated probabilities of a decline of the Nasdaq-100 over four weeks, and compared it with a Markov-switching model, with and without geolocated news processed in PostGIS. None of the models predicts the direction of the index over this horizon. Jev overestimates the probability of a decline by about ten percentage points (0.48 on average against an observed frequency of 0.38). A simple prior shift to the historical base rate reduces its ECE from 0.10 to 0.015 and turns a half-Kelly strategy that earned 3.1% per year into one that earns 14.5%, close to buy and hold.

Laya is an open-weights decision model built on the ModernBERT-large encoder (Convai Innovations, 2026; Warner et al., 2025). We fine-tuned it on the training period’s states with three heads: the nine-level move (labeled with the realized five-day move), a five-level magnitude head (the size of the same-day move) and, for the post-reaction reading, a three-class continuation head. It was trained once (one seed, one epoch) with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) and early stopping on val-A, and one temperature per head was fitted on val-A; the pre-registered second and third seeds are robustness runs (Section ).

The pre-registered calibration metric is the expected calibration error (Pakdaman Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017): the pre-open reading’s nine levels are grouped into three classes (a fall, no move and a rise, split at half a typical daily move), and the top class’s stated probability is compared with its hit rate against the realized five-day move, in 15 equal-width bins. Laya-Fin’s error is small (0.057) only because its probabilities barely leave the validation base rates: its log-loss improves on them by 0.001. The commercial models are overconfident. Their stated probabilities overstate their hit rates, with errors from 0.209 to 0.361 and negative log-loss skill, and a single temperature fitted on val-A lowers d1-ultra’s error from 0.260 to 0.155 (Appendix Table and Figure ). Calibration does not come with the decision-model interface; it has to be checked.

We train *System-1 decision models*, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). keenable.title: Boom-Busty Marketron as a Model of Market Dynamics: How Investor-Market Reflexivity Amplifies Non-Equilibrium
keenable.snippet: We introduce the Boom-Busty Marketron, a model of a multi-asset market in which the demand of a single collective investor moves prices and itself depends on market performance. This creates an investor-market reflexive loop in the spirit of Soros’s theory. The market state is stationary without being at equilibrium: a non-equilibrium steady state (NESS), with broken detailed balance and a probability current circulating between mispricing, demand and volatility. While stochastic volatility with the leverage effect already breaks detailed balance and makes the market dynamics irreversible, the investor-market loop pushes the market further away from equilibrium. Calibrated to the S&P 500 from 1996 to 2024 by simulated moments, the model reproduces the stylized facts of returns together with quantitative metrics of the market, including cross-sectional ones, and its return and cycle statistics stay stationary for a century and a half on the 1996–2010 inputs. Its central emergent behavior is a boom-bust cycle, whose frequency meets the S&P’s within one-sigma ranges.

keenable-realtime.title: Are Calibrated Decision Models Calibrated on Markets? Geolocated News, Markov Switching and a System One Model for Nasdaq-100 Allocation
keenable-realtime.snippet: Portfolio allocation is driven by probabilities of losses, not only by forecasts of the direction (up/down) of the market. A decision model such as Jev returns a probability for a yes/no question and has been reported to be well calibrated on a set of benchmarks. However, the model's calibration against realised market outcomes has not been tested. In this study, every Friday we ask whether the Nasdaq-100 will close lower four weeks later and compare a two-regime Markov-switching model estimated on data from 1990 to 2026, Jev reading weekly headlines and geolocated news features computed with spatial queries in PostGIS, and their combination. A knowledge probe shows that Jev knows events up to late 2024, so we evaluate it on 88 weeks from January 2025 onwards. None of the models predicts the direction better than the historical base rate. A key finding is that raw Jev overestimates the probability of a decline: its mean forecast is 0.48 against an observed frequency of 0.38, and its ECE is 0.10. A prior shift to the historical base rate, which uses no outcomes from the test period, lowers the ECE to 0.015. In contrast, Platt scaling, isotonic regression and the combination with the Markov model all make the forecasts worse. In a half-Kelly allocation, the raw Jev strategy returns 3.1% per year, whereas after the prior shift it returns 14.5%; a simple buy-and-hold strategy in QQQ returns 15.3% per year. The Markov model forecasts large declines (more than 10%) well, with an AUC of 0.81, and its strategy has the highest Sharpe ratio over 1999-2026. Asked about such a large decline (base rate 4%), raw Jev forecasts 16-24% on average, and the same prior shift removes this offset. The practical lesson is that decision-model probabilities must be anchored to the base rate of the market event before they are used to size positions.

keenable-realtime.title: Abstract
keenable-realtime.snippet:
### Decision model (Jev)
Jev is a “System One” decision model: instead of generating text, it returns a probability for a yes/no question (TypeSafe,, 2026; Deußer et al.,, 2026). We query version typesafe/jev-1.14-20261014 through the OpenRouter Decisions API with one fixed question for all weeks and inputs: *“Given the information available on [date] (a Friday), will the Nasdaq-100 index close lower 4 weeks later than it closed on [date]?”*, with the criteria “closes lower” (true) and “closes at the same level or higher” (false). The output p_t^(Jev) is the probability of “true”. We query Jev with four alternative inputs: (i) the 50 most widely published English-language headlines of the week (25 on economy and markets, 25 on conflict and geopolitics; see Data); (ii) the same headlines plus a JSON object with the GDELT features of the seven regions and their percentiles relative to past weeks; (iii) this JSON object alone; and (iv) a JSON object with Nasdaq-100 returns over 1, 4, 13 and 52 weeks, the 13-week volatility and the drawdown from the 52-week high (no index level, so that the input does not reveal the date). All 373 queries were made on 27 October 2026 and cost USD 0.017 in total (about USD 0.00005 per query).

We tested whether Jev, a decision model advertised as calibrated, gives calibrated probabilities of a decline of the Nasdaq-100 over four weeks, and compared it with a Markov-switching model, with and without geolocated news processed in PostGIS. None of the models predicts the direction of the index over this horizon. Jev overestimates the probability of a decline by about ten percentage points (0.48 on average against an observed frequency of 0.38). A simple prior shift to the historical base rate reduces its ECE from 0.10 to 0.015 and turns a half-Kelly strategy that earned 3.1% per year into one that earns 14.5%, close to buy and hold.

Laya is an open-weights decision model built on the ModernBERT-large encoder (Convai Innovations, 2026; Warner et al., 2025). Laya-Fin’s error is small (0.057) only because its probabilities barely leave the validation base rates: its log-loss improves on them by 0.001. The commercial models are overconfident. Their stated probabilities overstate their hit rates, with errors from 0.209 to 0.361 and negative log-loss skill, and a single temperature fitted on val-A lowers d1-ultra’s error from 0.260 to 0.155 (Appendix Table and Figure ). Calibration does not come with the decision-model interface; it has to be checked.

Interpretable Allocation and Model-Predictive Rebalancing of Equity Portfolios, Tested on Real and Synthetic Markets
Abstract
A live equity portfolio poses three problems: which stocks to hold, when to trade, and whether the strategy holds up beyond the observed market. We built one system for all three and tested it on 373 US equities, calibrated on 2014–2024 and traded January 2025 to September 2026. A selection rule chose stocks by score, by a bandit or at random, and one of seven weighting rules, four consumer-theory utilities and three standard portfolios, set share counts under limits on budget, single-stock weight, portfolio volatility and turnover, with each stock’s preference weight a bounded score of its trend, market beta and the market’s recent direction. A model-predictive controller forecast portfolio value with a multi-asset geometric Brownian motion and re-planned at its horizon, when the value left its forecast band, or at a drawdown stop. To probe deeper declines than the real window held, we also ran the system on simulated markets from per-asset hidden Markov generators with jumps, linked by market and sector factors. On real prices, the stocks chosen mattered more to terminal wealth than the weighting rule, and the early re-plans shrank the worst drawdown in most rule combinations against a fixed calendar without consistently raising wealth. In the deepest simulated declines, every combination, random picks included, ended above simulated SPY and the equal-weight universe in the median, even without early re-plans, so the margin came from shared parts of the system, not from stock selection or re-plan timing.

parallel.title: Markov Switching | Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Economics and Finance | Oxford Academic
parallel.snippet:
Abstract

Markov switching models are a family of models that introduces time variation in the parameters in the form of their state, or regime-specific values. This time variation is governed by a latent discrete-valued stochastic process with limited memory. More specifically, the current value of the state indicator is determined by the value of the state indicator from the previous period only implying the Markov property. A transition matrix characterizes the properties of the Markov process by determining with what probability each of the states can be visited next period conditionally on the state in the current period. This setup decides on the two main advantages of the Markov switching models: the estimation of the probability of state occurrences in each of the sample periods by using filtering and smoothing methods and the estimation of the state-specific parameters. These two features open the possibility for interpretations of the parameters associated with specific regimes combined with the corresponding regime probabilities.
The most commonly applied models from this family are those that presume a finite number of regimes and the exogeneity of the Markov process, which is defined as its independence from the model’s unpredictable innovations. In many such applications, the desired properties of the Markov switching model have been obtained either by imposing appropriate restrictions on transition probabilities or by introducing the time dependence of these probabilities determined by explanatory variables or functions of the state indicator. One of the extensions of this basic specification includes infinite hidden Markov models that provide great flexibility and excellent forecasting performance by allowing the number of states to go to infinity. Another extension, the endogenous Markov switching model, explicitly relates the state indicator to the model’s innovations, making it more interpretable and offering promising avenues for development.

Abstract

Since the 2008 financial crisis, agent-based models (ABMs), which account for out-of-equilibrium dynamics, heterogeneous preferences, time horizons and strategies, have often been envisioned as the new frontier that could revolutionise and displace the more standard models and tools in economics. While Jev is one implementation, we can think of this class of models as **calibrated decision models**.
*Decision* means the goal is to select from a list of options, *not to generate text*.

## Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the MarketThanks: Code availability: https://github.com/AmirDehkordi/NewsAction. The data are private and are not redistributed (Appendix ).

November 2026

###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision models, non-generative language models that return probabilities for typed questions, reading news about S&P 500 stocks: an open-weights model we fine-tuned on 2024–2025 data, three commercial models and standard baselines. The fine-tuned model’s signal replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but fell to 0.020 (t=1.7t=1.7) on the blinded January–July 2026 test. The commercial models’ readings line up with the overnight move to the open (information coefficient 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after it, so the news is priced by the time a trader can act on it at the open. No model can tell over- from under-reaction, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. Commercial models identify masked companies in 62% to 74% of cases against a 28% baseline: masking hides names, not companies. The market reads the news first.

We've added seven market regime strategies to the Strategies catalogue. After every market close, each one asks a single question: is the market calm or turbulent? **A market regime is a defined description of market behavior over a chosen horizon.** It might describe direction, volatility, liquidity or the way price rotates around an average. The purpose is to make strategy decisions testable: what changes when the environment changes, and does that change improve results after costs?

Regimes are estimates, not permanent market identities. A stock can trend upward on a daily chart while moving sideways intraday. A high-volatility market can trend strongly or swing repeatedly in both directions. Separating these dimensions is more useful than assigning one label such as “bullish” to every decision.

TypeSafe AI emerged from stealth with $40 million in seed funding led by DCVC and released **Jev**, the first publicly available System One model — a frontier-class AI that generates no text at all, returning typed decisions and calibrated probabilities instead. Weeks earlier, Convai Innovations had already published **Laya**: the same architectural idea, the same three decision primitives, the same training method family — but with Apache 2.0 weights anyone can download and run.

They are close cousins on paper and near-opposites in procurement. Jev is a hosted API. Laya is a file you hold. For a ministry, a statistical office, or a market-surveillance authority, that difference decides whether the technology is admissible at all.

## What a System One model actually is

Every mainstream large language model — GPT, Claude, Gemini, the open Llama family — works the same way: it generates text one token at a time, and your software then has to parse meaning back out of that string. The model writes the answer, and you hope your parser agrees with it.

A System One model inverts the pipeline. You send a block of program state plus a set of **typed questions**, and the model evaluates all of them in a single parallel pass, returning structured values with probabilities. There is nothing to parse, because nothing was generated. The output is already in the shape your code branches on.

The category name comes from Daniel Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow — System 1 being fast, intuitive judgment; System 2 being slow deliberation. The bet is that most software decisions need the first, not the second.

ultimate.title: Are Calibrated Decision Models Calibrated on Markets? Geolocated News, Markov Switching and a System One Model for Nasdaq-100 Allocation
ultimate.snippet: Portfolio allocation is driven by probabilities of losses, not only by forecasts of the direction (up/down) of the market. A decision model such as Jev returns a probability for a yes/no question and has been reported to be well calibrated on a set of benchmarks. However, the model's calibration against realised market outcomes has not been tested. In this study, every Friday we ask whether the Nasdaq-100 will close lower four weeks later and compare a two-regime Markov-switching model estimated on data from 1990 to 2026, Jev reading weekly headlines and geolocated news features computed with spatial queries in PostGIS, and their combination. A knowledge probe shows that Jev knows events up to late 2024, so we evaluate it on 88 weeks from January 2025 onwards. None of the models predicts the direction better than the historical base rate. A key finding is that raw Jev overestimates the probability of a decline: its mean forecast is 0.48 against an observed frequency of 0.38, and its ECE is 0.10. A prior shift to the historical base rate, which uses no outcomes from the test period, lowers the ECE to 0.015. In contrast, Platt scaling, isotonic regression and the combination with the Markov model all make the forecasts worse. In a half-Kelly allocation, the raw Jev strategy returns 3.1% per year, whereas after the prior shift it returns 14.5%; a simple buy-and-hold strategy in QQQ returns 15.3% per year. The Markov model forecasts large declines (more than 10%) well, with an AUC of 0.81, and its strategy has the highest Sharpe ratio over 1999-2026. Asked about such a large decline (base rate 4%), raw Jev forecasts 16-24% on average, and the same prior shift removes this offset. The practical lesson is that decision-model probabilities must be anchored to the base rate of the market event before they are used to size positions.

### Decision model (Jev)
Jev is a “System One” decision model: instead of generating text, it returns a probability for a yes/no question (TypeSafe,, 2026; Deußer et al.,, 2026). We query version typesafe/jev-1.14-20261014 through the OpenRouter Decisions API with one fixed question for all weeks and inputs: *“Given the information available on [date] (a Friday), will the Nasdaq-100 index close lower 4 weeks later than it closed on [date]?”*, with the criteria “closes lower” (true) and “closes at the same level or higher” (false). The output p_t^(Jev) is the probability of “true”. We query Jev with four alternative inputs: (i) the 50 most widely published English-language headlines of the week (25 on economy and markets, 25 on conflict and geopolitics; see Data); (ii) the same headlines plus a JSON object with the GDELT features of the seven regions and their percentiles relative to past weeks; (iii) this JSON object alone; and (iv) a JSON object with Nasdaq-100 returns over 1, 4, 13 and 52 weeks, the 13-week volatility and the drawdown from the 52-week high (no index level, so that the input does not reveal the date). All 373 queries were made on 27 October 2026 and cost USD 0.017 in total (about USD 0.00005 per query).

We tested whether Jev, a decision model advertised as calibrated, gives calibrated probabilities of a decline of the Nasdaq-100 over four weeks, and compared it with a Markov-switching model, with and without geolocated news processed in PostGIS. None of the models predicts the direction of the index over this horizon. Jev overestimates the probability of a decline by about ten percentage points (0.48 on average against an observed frequency of 0.38). A simple prior shift to the historical base rate reduces its ECE from 0.10 to 0.015 and turns a half-Kelly strategy that earned 3.1% per year into one that earns 14.5%, close to buy and hold.

ultimate.snippet:
Laya is an open-weights decision model built on the ModernBERT-large encoder (Convai Innovations, 2026; Warner et al., 2025). We fine-tuned it on the training period’s states with three heads: the nine-level move (labeled with the realized five-day move), a five-level magnitude head (the size of the same-day move) and, for the post-reaction reading, a three-class continuation head. It was trained once (one seed, one epoch) with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) and early stopping on val-A, and one temperature per head was fitted on val-A; the pre-registered second and third seeds are robustness runs (Section ).

The pre-registered calibration metric is the expected calibration error (Pakdaman Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017): the pre-open reading’s nine levels are grouped into three classes (a fall, no move and a rise, split at half a typical daily move), and the top class’s stated probability is compared with its hit rate against the realized five-day move, in 15 equal-width bins. Laya-Fin’s error is small (0.057) only because its probabilities barely leave the validation base rates: its log-loss improves on them by 0.001. The commercial models are overconfident. Their stated probabilities overstate their hit rates, with errors from 0.209 to 0.361 and negative log-loss skill, and a single temperature fitted on val-A lowers d1-ultra’s error from 0.260 to 0.155 (Appendix Table and Figure ). Calibration does not come with the decision-model interface; it has to be checked.

ultimate.title: Honest Small Decision Models for Finance: Scale, Specialization Collapse, and Mixed-Corpus Remediation
ultimate.snippet: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train *System-1 decision models*, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9–45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37–0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043–0.044 at 9–32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.

ultimate.title: Boom-Busty Marketron as a Model of Market Dynamics: How Investor-Market Reflexivity Amplifies Non-Equilibrium
ultimate.snippet: We introduce the Boom-Busty Marketron, a model of a multi-asset market in which the demand of a single collective investor moves prices and itself depends on market performance. This creates an investor-market reflexive loop in the spirit of Soros’s theory. The market state is stationary without being at equilibrium: a non-equilibrium steady state (NESS), with broken detailed balance and a probability current circulating between mispricing, demand and volatility.
